```{r setup}
library(mbmm)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

auc <- function(score, positive) {
  r <- rank(score)
  np <- sum(positive)
  nn <- sum(!positive)
  (sum(r[positive]) - np * (np + 1) / 2) / (np * nn)
}
```

## What this vignette must establish

**Scientific question:** does assignment to a vaccine arm change the
probability that a booster produces a positive durable antibody gain?

**Why MBMM:** durability is a property of an underlying plateau, not of one
observed visit. A short-lived peak can be large even when the long-lived level
does not improve.

**Route II:** there is no labelled reference population. Before examining the
outcomes, state 1 is defined as the region

\[
S_1=\{g>0\},\qquad g=\log_{10}(D_1/C_1),
\]

where $C_1$ is the long-lived level after prime and $D_1$ is the long-lived
level after boost. A marginal kinetic population is estimated and then
restricted to $S_1$ or its complement.

Because the data are simulated, success can be checked against the known
state and known gate. MBMM should recover the arm effect, classify the latent
region accurately, and retain adequate estimated mass on both sides of the
prespecified boundary.

## The hierarchy in scientific language

| MBMM object | Meaning in this simulation |
|---|---|
| $Y_i$ | repeated antibody measurements spanning prime and boost |
| $Z_i=1$ | the participant's durable gain satisfies $g>0$ |
| $Z_i=0$ | the durable gain satisfies $g\leq0$ |
| $x_i$ | randomised arm indicator |
| $\Pr(Z_i=1\mid x_i)$ | logistic gate with true intercept $-1$ and arm slope $2$ |
| $G$ | marginal population over $(g,m_s)$, estimated without state labels |
| $G_1,G_0$ | $G$ restricted and renormalised on $S_1$ and $S_0$ |

The boundary at zero is fixed by the biological question. It is not tuned to
maximise separation or significance.

## Mechanistic trajectory: the prime-boost antibody ODE

Between immunisations, the Andraud model satisfies

\[
\dot S=-m_sS,\qquad \dot A=W_l+S-m_AA,
\]

where $S$ is short-lived antibody production and $A$ is the measured antibody
level. The solution is a sum of exponential components. The boost changes the
short- and long-lived production fluxes; the long-lived asymptotes before and
after boost are $C_1=W_l/m_A$ and
$D_1=(W_l+\Delta W_l)/m_A$.

`andraud_trajectory()` evaluates the closed-form trajectory using the more
interpretable levels $A_0,C_1,C_2,D_1,D_2$ and the short-lived decay $m_s$.
Here only $g$ and $m_s$ vary so that the Route II construction stays visible.

## Simulate the known gate and kinetic truth

```{r truth}
set.seed(22)
n <- 120
arm <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
alpha_true <- -1
beta_true <- 2
pi_true <- plogis(alpha_true + beta_true * arm)
z <- rbinom(n, 1, pi_true)

c(true_probability_control = plogis(alpha_true),
  true_probability_vaccine = plogis(alpha_true + beta_true),
  realised_state1 = sum(z))
```

Create a fixed grid over durable gain and decay. Positive gains are drawn from
the positive part of the grid and non-positive gains from its complement.
Both states share the same decay grid.

```{r candidates}
G <- seq(-0.8, 0.8, by = 0.05)
MS <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.5)
candidates <- expand.grid(g = G, ms = MS)
candidates$A0 <- 400
candidates$C1 <- 900
candidates$C2 <- 0.35 * candidates$C1
candidates$D1 <- candidates$C1 * 10^candidates$g
candidates$D2 <- 0.70 * candidates$D1

w_positive_g <- dnorm(G, 0.35, 0.15) * (G > 0)
w_nonpositive_g <- dnorm(G, -0.25, 0.18) * (G <= 0)
w_positive_g <- w_positive_g / sum(w_positive_g)
w_nonpositive_g <- w_nonpositive_g / sum(w_nonpositive_g)

atom <- integer(n)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  gain_index <- sample(seq_along(G), 1,
                       prob = if (z[i]) w_positive_g else w_nonpositive_g)
  decay_index <- sample(seq_along(MS), 1)
  atom[i] <- gain_index + (decay_index - 1L) * length(G)
}
```

```{r simulate}
times <- c(0, 1, 2.8, 3.7, 8.4, 14, 19.6)
trajectory <- function(time, theta) {
  andraud_trajectory(time, theta$A0, theta$C1, theta$C2,
                     theta$D1, theta$D2, theta$ms)
}

obs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  mu <- trajectory(times, candidates[atom[i], ])
  data.frame(id = i, time = times,
             value = 10^(log10(mu) + rnorm(length(times), 0, 0.12)))
}))
```

```{r trajectory-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.alt="Twelve simulated prime-boost antibody trajectories split by whether their true durable gain is non-positive or positive."}
plot_ids <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(n), z), head, 6))
plot_obs <- subset(obs, id %in% plot_ids)
plot_obs$state <- factor(z[plot_obs$id], levels = 0:1,
                         labels = c("State 0: g <= 0", "State 1: g > 0"))

ggplot(plot_obs, aes(time, value, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~state) +
  labs(x = "Time since prime (months)", y = "Antibody level (log scale)",
       title = "Simulated prime-boost trajectories by the known durable state")
```

The true state is used only to evaluate recovery. The MBMM fitting code below
does not receive `z`.

## Score all candidates, then fit honest marginal banks

```{r likelihood}
LL <- trajectory_loglik(obs, candidates, trajectory, sigma = 0.12)
loo <- bank_loo(LL, lambda = 1)
dim(loo$weights)
```

`LL[i, j]` is the log likelihood of participant $i$ under kinetic atom $j$.
`bank_loo()` refits the marginal weights 120 times: the weights in row $i$
were estimated using every participant except $i$. This is essential because
the same cohort supplies the marginal kinetic population and is then scored
against it.

Unlike Route I, the bank is not a state-1 bank. It estimates the combined
population across both sides of the boundary.

## Restrict the marginal population to the two states

```{r restrict}
state1_region <- candidates$g > 0

score_region <- function(region) {
  vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    restricted <- restrict_bank(loo$weights[i, ], region)$weights
    class_loglik(LL[i, , drop = FALSE], restricted)[1]
  }, numeric(1))
}

l1 <- score_region(state1_region)
l0 <- score_region(!state1_region)
mass1 <- rowSums(loo$weights[, state1_region, drop = FALSE])

summary(mass1)
```

`restrict_bank()` first computes the fold-specific mass in a region and then
renormalises the weights inside that region. Restriction divides by region
mass, so near-zero mass would make a Route II result unstable. Here every fold
keeps substantial mass on both sides.

The following plot distinguishes three different objects: the population used
to generate atoms, the finite realised sample of atoms, and the average
leave-one-out estimate. They need not match point for point in a finite sample.

```{r bank-comparison, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 9, fig.alt=c("Generating population weights over durable gain and decay.", "Finite realised atom frequencies over durable gain and decay.", "Average leave-one-out estimated weights over durable gain and decay.")}
mean_pi <- mean(pi_true)
true_gain_weight <- mean_pi * w_positive_g +
  (1 - mean_pi) * w_nonpositive_g
true_atom_weight <- rep(true_gain_weight / length(MS), times = length(MS))
realised_atom_weight <- tabulate(atom, nbins = nrow(candidates)) / n
estimated_atom_weight <- colMeans(loo$weights)

p_truth <- plot_bank(candidates, true_atom_weight, "g", "ms") +
  labs(title = "Generating population")
p_realised <- plot_bank(candidates, realised_atom_weight, "g", "ms") +
  labs(title = "Finite realised participants")
p_estimated <- plot_bank(candidates, estimated_atom_weight, "g", "ms") +
  labs(title = "Estimated marginal population")

print(p_truth)
print(p_realised)
print(p_estimated)
```

## Fit and interpret the arm gate

```{r gate}
X <- cbind(intercept = 1, vaccine_arm = arm)
fit <- fit_gate(l1, l0, X, firth = TRUE)
oracle <- coef(glm(z ~ arm, family = binomial()))

coefficient_check <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("Generating truth", "Oracle using true state", "MBMM"),
  intercept = c(alpha_true, oracle[1], fit$gamma[1]),
  arm_slope = c(beta_true, oracle[2], fit$gamma[2])
)
coefficient_check
```

Firth penalisation is used because accurate state evidence can create near
separation. The oracle again shows the finite-sample logistic result that
would be obtained if the state were observed.

```{r responsibility-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.alt="Posterior probabilities of positive durable gain grouped by the known simulated parameter region."}
plot_responsibility(fit, z) +
  labs(title = "Responsibility compared with the known parameter region")
```

```{r gate-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.alt="True and estimated probabilities of positive durable gain in the control and vaccine arms."}
plot_gate(fit, arm, truth = z, true_probability = pi_true) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:1, labels = c("Control", "Vaccine")) +
  labs(x = "Randomised arm", y = "Probability of positive durable gain",
       title = "Estimated and generating gate probabilities")
```

## Did MBMM recover what it should?

```{r recovery}
estimated_probability <- tapply(fit$pi, arm, mean)
true_probability <- c(control = plogis(alpha_true),
                      vaccine = plogis(alpha_true + beta_true))

recovery <- c(
  true_arm_slope = beta_true,
  oracle_arm_slope = unname(oracle[2]),
  mbmm_arm_slope = unname(fit$gamma[2]),
  state_AUC = auc(fit$w, z == 1),
  uncertain_responsibilities = sum(fit$w > 0.1 & fit$w < 0.9),
  minimum_state1_mass = min(mass1),
  maximum_state1_mass = max(mass1)
)
round(recovery, 3)
rbind(truth = true_probability, estimated = estimated_probability)
```

```{r permutation-test}
test <- gate_test(l1, l0, X, firth = TRUE, B = 199, seed = 1)
test
```

With `firth = TRUE`, the statistic is a difference in penalised objectives,
not an ordinary likelihood-ratio statistic. The reported p-value comes from
permuting the arm rows while keeping the trajectory-derived class likelihoods
fixed.

```{r executable-checks}
stopifnot(
  recovery["state_AUC"] > 0.9,
  recovery["mbmm_arm_slope"] > 0,
  abs(recovery["mbmm_arm_slope"] - recovery["oracle_arm_slope"]) < 0.75,
  recovery["minimum_state1_mass"] > 0.1,
  recovery["maximum_state1_mass"] < 0.9,
  recovery["uncertain_responsibilities"] > 0,
  test$p_value <= 0.05
)
```

## What changed from Route I?

Route I estimated a pure state-1 population from independent labelled donors
and paired it with a separate background state. Route II instead estimated one
marginal population from the analysis cohort, cross-fitted it, and restricted
it to a prespecified region and its complement. The gate calculation is the
same after the two class likelihoods have been formed.

This controlled example checks that Route II recovers its known region and arm
effect. A real analysis must additionally justify the biological boundary,
identifiability of $g$, candidate coverage, the observation model,
exchangeability across participants, and adequate region mass in every fold.
Return to the [scientific and practical guide](mbmm.html), or compare the
[Route I simulation](pipeline.html).
